title: In, to, from
goal: Use Norwegian prepositions for place and time — and master a distinction English has almost lost: words for places change form when there is movement.
bekal: talking about time with *i*, *på*, *om* and *for … siden*
wave: Review **unit 9** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Name each object in both orders — *genseren min* and *min genser*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvor skal du?
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. Budi is tying his shoelaces in the hallway when Ingrid appears with a big backpack on her back.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvor skal du med den sekken?
lines.id: Where are you off to with that backpack?
lines.literal: where shall you with that backpack?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Hjem til foreldrene mine. De bor på Hamar.
lines.id: Home to my parents. They live in Hamar.
lines.literal: home to parents-the mine. they live on Hamar.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: På. Ikke spør hvorfor. Vi sier i Oslo, men på Hamar.
lines.id: *På*. Don't ask why. We say *i Oslo* but *på Hamar*.
lines.literal: on. not ask why. we say in Oslo, but on Hamar.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Og du er hjemme i to dager?
lines.id: And you're home for two days?
lines.literal: and you are at-home in two days?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Tre. Jeg kommer tilbake på søndag kveld.
lines.id: Three. I'll be back Sunday evening.
lines.literal: three. I come back on Sunday evening.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ja. Det går fra Oslo S om førti minutter. Hva gjør du i helga?
lines.id: Yes. It leaves Oslo S in forty minutes. What are you doing this weekend?
lines.literal: yes. it goes from Oslo S in forty minutes. what do you in weekend-the?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg skal være hjemme. Kanskje til Ahmad på lørdag.
lines.id: I'm staying home. Maybe going to Ahmad's on Saturday.
lines.literal: I shall be at-home. maybe to Ahmad on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Hos Ahmad, mener du. «Til» er veien, «hos» er huset.
lines.id: *Hos* Ahmad, you mean. *Til* is the road, *hos* is the house.
lines.literal: at Ahmad, mean you. "to" is road-the, "at" is house-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg går **til** Ahmad, og så er jeg **hos** Ahmad?
lines.id: I *go to* Ahmad's, and then I'm *at* Ahmad's?
lines.literal: I walk to Ahmad, and then am I at Ahmad?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Nå har du det. God helg! Nå må jeg løpe ut.
lines.id: Now you've got it. Have a good weekend! Now I have to run.
lines.literal: now have you it. good weekend! now must I run out.

notes: **Prepositions are the part of a language that maps least one-to-one.** Don't hunt for big rules; what works is memorizing whole phrases. Every language is like this, English included — try explaining to a foreigner why it's "on the bus" but "in the car".

**På Hamar, i Oslo.** Norwegian uses *på* for some places and *i* for others, and the split is mostly history, not logic. Rough pattern: *i* for big cities and countries, *på* for islands, small inland towns and high places. When in doubt, use *i* — it's right most often.

**Hjem versus hjemme** is a required distinction. *Hjem* is used when there is **movement toward** (jeg går hjem — I'm going home), *hjemme* when you are **already there** (jeg er hjemme — I'm at home). English does the same with "home" vs "at home", but Norwegian extends the idea to many more words.

**Til versus hos** follows the same split. *Jeg går **til** Ahmad* — I'm heading to Ahmad's place. *Jeg er **hos** Ahmad* — I'm at Ahmad's place. *Hos* works like French *chez*; English has no single word for it and uses "at …'s".
**Skal du med toget?** — the verb *å gå* or *å reise* is often dropped entirely after *skal*. *Jeg skal til Bergen* is complete and means "I'm going to Bergen". This shortcut is used all the time.
**Om førti minutter** = in forty minutes (from now), **for førti minutter siden** = forty minutes ago. Two phrases that often get mixed up; learn them as a pair.

grammars.title: Four prepositions of place
body: These four cover most everyday needs. Look at the last column — that's where the difference shows.

head: Preposition
Meaning
Used for
Example
rows: *i Norge, i Oslo, i huset, i bilen*
*på skolen, på bordet, på Hamar, på Island*
movement toward a place or person

after: ⚠️ **Institutions always take *på***, even where English uses "in": *på skolen* (at school), *på universitetet* (at university), *på jobb* (at work), *på sykehuset* (in the hospital), *på kino* (at the movies), *på kafé*. This is a big group and the most common mistake.
*Å gå på skolen* means "to go to school" as an activity; *å gå til skolen* means "to walk to the school building". The difference is real, and Norwegians hear it.
Transport takes *med*, and the noun takes its ending: *med **toget***, *med **bussen***, *med **bilen***, *med **fly***. The last one is the exception and stands bare.

grammars.title: Movement versus place: pairs to memorize
body: This is the truly new part for English speakers. Norwegian has **two different forms** for words like "out" (going) and "out" (being there), and choosing the wrong one makes the sentence sound broken.
after: Notice the pattern: the "already there" form is almost always **one syllable longer**. That's a shortcut you can hold on to.

*Jeg går **hjem*** (I'm going home) versus *jeg er **hjemme*** (I'm at home). *Kom **inn**!* (come in!) versus *han er **inne*** (he's inside). *Kom **hit**!* (come here!) versus *jeg er **her*** (I'm here).
English has leftovers of the same system in *hither/thither/whither*, but they died long ago. Norwegian still uses it fully every day.

grammars.title: Prepositions of time
body: These can't be translated one-to-one at all, so learn them as whole phrases.

head: Phrase
Meaning
Partner
rows: in the mornings / in the evenings

after: The three rows most often confused are *om ti minutter*, *for ti minutter siden* and *i ti minutter*. Say all three in a row now, then again tomorrow.
*Om* does two different jobs: it marks repeated habits (*om morgenen*) **and** time ahead (*om ti minutter*). The noun form tells you which — the *-en* ending signals a habit.

blocks.text: Notice the preposition attached to each place. The preposition is part of the vocabulary — learn them together, not separately.

*På butikken* and *i butikken* are both correct and mean slightly different things: the first means "out shopping", the second "inside the building". Differences this thin are why prepositions can't be learned by rules.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Describe your day from waking up to coming home, and name the preposition for each place: *Jeg går til bussen, jeg er på universitetet, jeg kommer hjem.*
Then say the eight movement/place pairs in a row: *hjem–hjemme, ut–ute, inn–inne, opp–oppe, ned–nede, bort–borte, hit–her, dit–der*. Repeat until you don't have to think.
If you use the wrong preposition, Norwegians almost always still understand. If you use *hjemme* when you mean *hjem*, they pause for a second. That's the order of importance.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with *i*, *på*, *til* or *hos*.

items: Han er ____ i dag. (hjem or hjemme)
We're taking the train to Bergen.
The bus comes in ten minutes.
Ten minutes ago he was here.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: toget / med / Bergen / til / vi / reiser
Ahmad / kveld / hos / er / jeg / i

answers: i — på — til — på — hos — til
hjem — hjemme — inn — ute — hit — der
Jeg bor i Oslo. — Hun jobber på sykehuset. — Vi reiser til Bergen med toget. — På lørdag er jeg hos Ahmad. — Bussen kommer om ti minutter. — For ti minutter siden var han her.
